claims.text: Money supply is the total stock of money in an economy at a point in time: the notes and coins in circulation plus the bank deposits that can be spent by card, cheque or transfer.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Monetary policy is the use of changes in interest rates, the money supply and the foreign exchange rate, carried out by the central bank, to influence the economy's performance.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The central bank carries out monetary policy by setting the rate at which it lends to commercial banks, whereas commercial banks take deposits and make loans; candidates often confuse the two.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The main measures of monetary policy are changes in interest rates; measures to control the growth of the money supply, such as selling government securities to banks or tightening the rules under which banks create new deposits through lending; and changes in the foreign exchange rate, which a central bank can influence by buying or selling its own currency with its foreign currency reserves.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A rise in the policy interest rate tends to raise loan rates and deposit rates together; borrowing and credit-financed spending tend to fall, saving tends to rise, and the growth of the money supply slows, while a cut works in the opposite direction.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Monetary policy measures work on the price and quantity of money - interest rates, the money supply and the exchange rate - whereas supply-side policy measures work on the economy's capacity to produce, such as worker training, roads and support for new equipment.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Interest-rate changes work through the whole banking system at once and reach households and firms across the economy, which is a strength of the measure.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Relying on interest-rate changes has drawbacks: the effects arrive with a delay, spending financed without bank credit responds less to the rate, and dearer borrowing may hold back investment and jobs.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Monetary policy bears most directly on the aim of price stability: raising interest rates tends to slow spending and the growth of the money supply, which eases upward pressure on prices, while lowering rates tends to encourage borrowing, spending and output growth, which supports jobs.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Monetary policy aimed at one aim can work against another: a rate rise that slows a rise in prices may also slow output growth and employment, and its effects differ between savers, who gain, and borrowers, who lose.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Price stability is the aim of keeping the rise in the general price level low and steady, and it is the macroeconomic aim monetary policy serves most directly.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Monetary policy touches the government's macroeconomic aims at different removes: price stability directly, and growth, employment and the external position indirectly, through spending, borrowing and exchange rates.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A central bank that sells its own currency for foreign currency tends to lower the exchange rate, making exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home, while one that buys its own currency with its reserves tends to raise the exchange rate, making exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper at home.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A rise in interest rates tends to narrow a current account deficit by slowing spending, including spending on imports, but it may also attract funds from abroad and raise the exchange rate, making exports dearer and imports cheaper; a lower exchange rate tends to narrow a deficit where demand for exports and imports is elastic enough to respond and supply can respond.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A rise in interest rates transfers income from borrowers to savers, which can widen the income gap where savers are better-off households, and may cost low-paid jobs first, while holding down inflation protects households on low or fixed incomes; a rate cut works the other way.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Interest rates are a monetary policy measure, changed through the central bank, whereas tax rates are a fiscal policy measure, set by the government in its budget; who sets the rate and who receives the payment tells them apart.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
